verses.text: Now in the twelfth month, which is the month Adar, on the thirteenth day of the month, when the king’s commandment and his decree came near to be put in execution, on the day that the enemies of the Jews hoped to conquer them, (but it was turned out the opposite happened, that the Jews conquered those who hated them),

the Jews gathered themselves together in their cities throughout all the provinces of the King Ahasuerus, to lay hands on those who wanted to harm them. No one could withstand them, because the fear of them had fallen on all the people.
All the princes of the provinces, the satraps, the governors, and those who did the king’s business helped the Jews, because the fear of Mordecai had fallen on them.
For Mordecai was great in the king’s house, and his fame went out throughout all the provinces; for the man Mordecai grew greater and greater.
The Jews struck all their enemies with the stroke of the sword, and with slaughter and destruction, and did what they wanted to those who hated them.
In the citadel of Susa, the Jews killed and destroyed five hundred men.
They killed Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha,
Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha,
Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai, and Vaizatha,
the ten sons of Haman the son of Hammedatha, the Jews’ enemy, but they didn’t lay their hand on the plunder.
On that day, the number of those who were slain in the citadel of Susa was brought before the king.

The king said to Esther the queen, “The Jews have slain and destroyed five hundred men in the citadel of Susa, including the ten sons of Haman; what then have they done in the rest of the king’s provinces! Now what is your petition? It shall be granted you. What is your further request? It shall be done.”
Then Esther said, “If it pleases the king, let it be granted to the Jews who are in Shushan to do tomorrow also according to today’s decree, and let Haman’s ten sons be hanged on the gallows.”
The king commanded this to be done. A decree was given out in Shushan; and they hanged Haman’s ten sons.
The Jews who were in Shushan gathered themselves together on the fourteenth day also of the month Adar, and killed three hundred men in Shushan; but they didn’t lay their hand on the plunder.

The other Jews who were in the king’s provinces gathered themselves together, defended their lives, had rest from their enemies, and killed seventy-five thousand of those who hated them; but they didn’t lay their hand on the plunder.
This was done on the thirteenth day of the month Adar; and on the fourteenth day of that month they rested and made it a day of feasting and gladness.

But the Jews who were in Shushan assembled together on the thirteenth and on the fourteenth days of the month; and on the fifteenth day of that month, they rested, and made it a day of feasting and gladness.

Therefore the Jews of the villages, who live in the unwalled towns, make the fourteenth day of the month Adar a day of gladness and feasting, a good day, and a day of sending presents of food to one another.
Mordecai wrote these things, and sent letters to all the Jews who were in all the provinces of the king Ahasuerus, both near and far,
to enjoin them that they should keep the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the month Adar yearly,

as the days in which the Jews had rest from their enemies, and the month which was turned to them from sorrow to gladness, and from mourning into a good day; that they should make them days of feasting and gladness, and of sending presents of food to one another, and gifts to the needy.
The Jews accepted the custom that they had begun, as Mordecai had written to them;
because Haman the son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had plotted against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast “Pur”, that is the lot, to consume them, and to destroy them;

but when this became known to the king, he commanded by letters that his wicked device, which he had devised against the Jews, should return on his own head, and that he and his sons should be hanged on the gallows.

Therefore they called these days “Purim”,  from the word “Pur.” Therefore because of all the words of this letter, and of that which they had seen concerning this matter, and that which had come to them,

the Jews established, and imposed on themselves, and on their descendants, and on all those who joined themselves to them, so that it should not fail, that they would keep these two days according to what was written, and according to its appointed time, every year;

and that these days should be remembered and kept throughout every generation, every family, every province, and every city; and that these days of Purim should not fail from among the Jews, nor their memory perish from their offspring,
Then Esther the queen, the daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew, wrote with all authority to confirm this second letter of Purim.
He sent letters to all the Jews, to the hundred twenty-seven provinces of the kingdom of Ahasuerus, with words of peace and truth,

to confirm these days of Purim in their appointed times, as Mordecai the Jew and Esther the queen had decreed, and as they had imposed upon themselves and their descendants, in the matter of the fastings and their cry.
The commandment of Esther confirmed these matters of Purim; and it was written in the book.

footnotes.content: The thirteenth of Adar had been marked as the day of the Jews' ruin. Instead, the Lord turned it upside down. I've seen Him do this—what we dread becomes the doorway to His deliverance. He works in the shadows until the very hour when fear turns to joy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Jews gathered their strength, not in arrogance but in defense of their very lives. When fear had gripped others, the Lord raised courage in His people. There's something holy in a community standing together for their own preservation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even the high officials of Persia—satraps and governors—helped the Jews, afraid of Mordecai's growing power. The Lord works through natural human respect and authority; sometimes deliverance comes through the very structures that seemed arrayed against us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mordecai's greatness was not sought but given by the Lord's hand. As a man honors God's faithfulness, his influence grows. I see in him a quiet dignity—one who did the right thing and let the King's own purpose accomplish the rest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Jews struck down their enemies—those who had sought their destruction. This is lawful judgment, not revenge; the Lord's hand restraining what would have destroyed His people. Justice is sometimes swift and sharp.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the citadel of Susa itself—the very seat of the king's power—five hundred enemies fell. The numbers show the scope of deliverance; what seemed an impossible tangle of power, the Lord untangled in a single day.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha—Haman's sons are named one by one. Even in a list, each death marks the end of a family line bent on murder. The hand of the Lord falls on those who scheme to destroy His people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha—more names fall. The catalog of these deaths is no small thing. Haman had believed his plot was hidden; the Lord knew every heart and exposed every thread of wickedness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai, Vaizatha—the list continues. Each name was a breath, a heartbeat, a soul bent against God's chosen. In one day, the threat that had seemed to close all doors was utterly dispelled.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The ten sons of Haman—all of them, every one—were struck down. And the Jews took no plunder; they defended their lives, not their greed. This restraint shows the difference between justice and mere violence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king learned the count—five hundred and ten in Susa alone. News travels to the throne itself, and the Lord's deliverance becomes a matter of public record. Hidden mercy becomes testimony.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king speaks to Esther with wonder: 'What have they done in the rest of the provinces?' His tone is not anger but amazement. He sees that the God of these people has moved His hand. Esther kneels before a king who has become her ally.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esther asks for one more day and for Haman's sons to be hanged on the gallows. Her request is measured and specific. The widow who came trembling before this king now asks for justice without apology. The Lord had given her both boldness and discernment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king commands it, and the decree is done. The bodies of Haman's ten sons hang as a sign to all: wickedness does not prosper hidden in the royal court. The Lord's justice is made visible.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: On the second day in Shushan, three hundred more fell. Again, the Jews laid hands only on those who hated them, and took no plunder. The discipline of their self-defense was as striking as its force.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In all the provinces, seventy-five thousand enemies fell. The size of this deliverance is almost beyond reckoning. And still the Jews took no plunder—they sought only rest and safety. Restraint in the hour of power marks a people walking with the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The thirteenth was a day of battle; the fourteenth became a day of feasting and gladness. The Lord gives rest after the struggle. There is wisdom in letting the dust settle and joy break through—not forgetting, but honoring the Lord's hand in deliverance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In Shushan itself, the fighting lasted longer—two days, with rest on the fifteenth. The city at the heart of empire experienced an extra day of the Lord's shaking. Feasting came when the danger was truly past.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The villages—the unwalled towns—the smaller places far from the city's power—they too celebrated. The custom spreads outward: the fourteenth becomes a day of gladness and gifts shared. The Lord's mercy reaches to the margins as well as the center.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mordecai writes letters to all the Jews throughout the provinces. He does not let this deliverance fade into memory; he anchors it in writing. Words make an act of the Lord permanent, so generations to come can know: He has saved His people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Keep the fourteenth and fifteenth days yearly—a command rooted in history. What began as a narrow escape becomes a calendar of remembrance. The Lord's people are invited to return again and again to this stone of witness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The month that turned from sorrow to gladness, from mourning to a good day—this is the shape of the Lord's work. Feasting, gifts, remembrance of His faithfulness. Joy and generosity spring up where despair had crouched.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Jews accepted this custom freely, by choice. They said yes to remembrance. Not a burden imposed, but a gift received and embraced. This is how the Lord works with His people—not by force, but by leading the heart to gratitude.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Haman cast the Pur—the lot—to consume and destroy them all. He believed chance was on his side; he did not know that the Lord sets all lots in His own hand. Every scheme unravels when the Lord has decided otherwise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king, by letter, commanded that Haman's wicked device return upon his own head. What was meant to destroy the Jews became the snare for the hunter. This is the Lord's way: the pit dug for others becomes the grave of the digger.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They called these days Purim, from the word 'Pur'—the lot. The very name that had meant their doom became the name of their deliverance. What we feared becomes the word by which we remember God's mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They established this for themselves and their descendants—a covenant written in their own hand. Not a law imposed, but a vow taken. The children yet unborn would inherit a memory of the Lord's faithfulness toward their people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every generation, every family, every province, every city—Purim reaches into every corner. The Lord's salvation was not for one time or one place, but for all His people, everywhere. His mercy echoes across time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esther and Mordecai write together with full authority. The queen and the wise counselor speak as one. Their bond, forged in faithfulness, becomes the seal upon this remembrance. Two voices, one testimony.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Letters sent to all one hundred twenty-seven provinces, words of peace and truth. The message goes out to the edges of the empire. Peace—a word that means more when it comes after the shadow of death.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The days of Purim are confirmed in their appointed times, rooted in fasting and crying—remembering the cost of deliverance. Joy and fasting are held together. We celebrate what was won, and remember how near the edge we stood.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esther's commandment confirmed these matters of Purim; it was written in the book. Readers today hear an echo in this: what the Lord does does not fade. Written down, it becomes a stone of witness for all who come after—a sign that God remembers His people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
